result.summary: Pausanias continues his tour of the Olympic victor statues, noting athletes, their sculptors and teachers, and the odd facts about them. He questions the tradition about Oebotas, and ends with the statue of Lysander set up by the Samians, which he uses to show how the Ionians court whoever is strongest.

scenes.title: Statues of boxers and pentathletes
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists statues of boys and men from Sicyon, Messene and Elis, with their victories, sculptors and sculptors' teachers.

scenes.title: The puzzle of Oebotas
scenes.summary: Pausanias shows that Oebotas, victor in the sixth Olympiad, could not have fought at Plataea, and says he need not believe every Greek tradition.

scenes.title: More victors and Caulonia
scenes.summary: Further statues are described, including Hysmon, whose training cured an illness, and Dicon, who changed his city for money. Pausanias digresses on the fall of Caulonia.

scenes.title: Lysander's statue and the Ionians
scenes.summary: The Samians' statue of Lysander and its inscriptions lead Pausanias to remark that the Ionians flatter whoever holds power: Alcibiades, Lysander, then Conon and Timotheus.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias states his method: he reports Greek traditions without necessarily believing them.
Cynical summary: men always court the strongest.

analysis.text: The passage shows Pausanias as a careful, critical antiquarian, checking dates and traditions against each other.
Statues at Olympia record athletes, cities and sculptor lineages, and show how politics shaped honors, such as Ionian flattery of Athens and then Sparta.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias traces teacher-pupil chains of sculptors, a rare source for dating Greek sculptors.

language_notes.text: "Votive offering" means a gift dedicated to a god in thanks or fulfilment of a vow; here a statue set up at Olympia.
"Pentathlum" is the pentathlon, a five-event contest (running, jumping, discus, javelin, wrestling).
The Lacedæmonians' defeat at Leuctra (371 BC) by Thebes broke Spartan power; Pausanias uses it to date the Elean expedition.
"Through 4 intermediate teachers" means a chain of four successive teacher-pupil links, spelled out in the next sentence.
"Got indemnity" means Leo obtained compensation from the two umpires who ruled against him, apparently for an unjust decision.
Plataea (479 BC) was the decisive land battle of the Persian Wars; Oebotas was said to have fought there, which the dates make impossible.
The Eleans were barred from the Isthmian games, by a tradition Pausanias recounts elsewhere; the people of Lepreus faced no such ban.
"Discharge" is a vague medical term for some bodily ailment; the exact illness is not specified.
"Dumb bells" here means halteres, stone or metal weights held in the hands by jumpers and athletes.
"Proclaimed" refers to the herald's announcement of a victor's name and city; Dicon changed the city announced.
The proverb "whitewashed two walls" means pleasing both sides, flattering rival parties in turn.
Conon's victory off Cnidus (394 BC) ended Spartan sea power, so the Ionians turned to honour him.

context_notes.text: Ptolemy I, a general of Alexander the Great, became king of Egypt; calling himself Macedonian stressed his Greek, Macedonian origin.
Lepreus was a town in Elis, in the western Peloponnese.
Elis administered the Olympic games, so its citizens often held athletic offices and trained youths.
Mardonius commanded the Persian army defeated at Plataea by the Greeks in 479 BC.
Pyrrhus of Epirus fought the Romans in Italy in the early 3rd century BC, allied with Tarentum.
Lysander was the Spartan admiral who defeated Athens at Aegospotami in 405 BC and was honoured by many Greek cities.

literary_notes.text: The chain of "was the pupil of" clauses mirrors the unbroken line of teaching it describes, giving the genealogy a rhythmic flow.
Praising Cratinus' beauty alongside his wrestling skill shows the Greek ideal of physical excellence in an athlete.
Pausanias speaks as a cautious historian, separating duty to record tradition from personal belief.
The remark that training was destined to bring victories anticipates his later success, making a cure the start of his glory.
Whitewashing two walls figures political flattery as decorating both sides' houses, a vivid image of Ionian opportunism.
Pausanias closes by turning the Samians' lofty praise into a general cynical judgment on human flattery of power.
